choiceExplanations.0: Snapshots provide point-in-time backup capability but do not provide automatic failover; restoring from a snapshot requires manual intervention and results in significant downtime, not meeting the automatic failover requirement.
choiceExplanations.1: A single EC2 instance provides no high availability or automatic failover capability, and EBS snapshots only provide backup functionality requiring manual restoration, which contradicts the automatic failover requirement.
choiceExplanations.2: Read replicas use asynchronous replication and are designed for read scaling, not automatic failover; promoting a read replica to primary requires manual intervention and application changes to update connection endpoints.

resources.title: Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS

question:
A global e-commerce site runs active applications in two AWS Regions. The business wants users to be routed to the closest healthy region and fail over automatically if one region becomes unhealthy.
Which Route 53 routing policy best fits?
explanation: Latency-based routing directs users to the region that provides the lowest latency, and health checks enable automatic failover away from unhealthy endpoints.

choiceExplanations.0: Weighted routing distributes traffic based on assigned proportions rather than routing users to the closest region, and without health checks there is no automatic failover when a region becomes unhealthy.
choiceExplanations.2: Geolocation routing directs users based on their geographic location rather than network latency to find the closest region, and without health checks it cannot automatically fail over when a region becomes unhealthy.
choiceExplanations.3: Simple routing returns all values in random order and does not support health check failover or any logic to route users to the closest or healthiest region, making it unsuitable for multi-region active-active deployments requiring automatic failover.

question:
A service runs on Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type across two AZs. The team needs tasks to be automatically replaced when they fail, and wants to maintain a desired number of running tasks.
Which ECS feature provides this behavior?
choices: An ECS service with a desired task count
explanation: An ECS service maintains the desired number of tasks and will replace failed tasks automatically. Health checks help ECS/ALB determine unhealthy tasks and trigger replacement.

choiceExplanations.1: Amazon ECR stores and distributes container images; it does not run tasks, so it cannot replace a failed task or hold a desired task count.
choiceExplanations.2: This feature allows you to run commands or get a shell inside a running container for debugging and troubleshooting purposes, but it does not provide any automatic task replacement or maintain desired task counts.
choiceExplanations.3: A task definition is a blueprint that describes container configurations such as CPU, memory, and image settings, but it does not manage task lifecycle or automatically replace failed tasks; an ECS service is required for that functionality.

question:
A web application is deployed on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The team wants unhealthy instances to be replaced automatically when they fail application-level health checks.
Which configuration should they implement?
choices: Enable detailed monitoring on EC2 instances only
Use a Network Load Balancer and disable health checks
Use Amazon CloudFront in front of the ALB and rely on edge caching
Turn on ELB health checks for the Auto Scaling group
explanation: The ALB target group health check detects application-level failures. When the Auto Scaling group is set to use ELB health checks, it replaces instances the load balancer reports as unhealthy; by default it would ignore them.

choiceExplanations.0: Detailed monitoring provides more frequent CloudWatch metrics (1-minute intervals) for EC2 system-level metrics like CPU and network, but it does not perform application-level health checks or trigger Auto Scaling to replace unhealthy instances based on application health.
choiceExplanations.1: Disabling health checks removes any signal that an instance is failing, so the Auto Scaling group would never learn that an instance should be replaced.
choiceExplanations.2: CloudFront is a CDN service that caches content at edge locations to improve performance, but it does not monitor instance health or integrate with Auto Scaling to replace unhealthy instances; cached content would simply mask backend failures temporarily.

resources.title: Health checks for instances in an Auto Scaling group

question:
A company needs to protect critical S3 objects from accidental overwrites and deletions, but they also want the ability to recover previous versions.
Which S3 feature best meets this requirement?
explanation: S3 versioning preserves multiple variants of an object in the same bucket, enabling recovery from accidental overwrites and deletions.

choiceExplanations.0: This feature speeds up content transfers to and from S3 by using Amazon CloudFront's globally distributed edge locations, but it does not provide any protection against accidental overwrites or deletions.
choiceExplanations.2: This feature shifts the cost of requests and data transfer to the requester instead of the bucket owner, but it has no capability to protect objects from being overwritten or deleted or to recover previous versions.
choiceExplanations.3: This feature allows you to host a static website directly from an S3 bucket by serving HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, but it provides no protection against accidental modifications or deletions and no version recovery capability.

resources.title: Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning

question:
A serverless workload writes items to DynamoDB. Occasionally, downstream processing fails and needs to be retried without losing events.
Which option provides the MOST resilient event-driven design?
choices: Trigger the Lambda function directly from an S3 bucket event notification
Write the items to DynamoDB and rely on manual reprocessing of any failures
Use DynamoDB Streams to trigger Lambda, with retries and an on-failure destination for failed records
Have the Lambda function poll DynamoDB every minute and scan the whole table
explanation: DynamoDB Streams provide an ordered change log for table modifications. The Lambda event source mapping retries failed batches and can send details of records it could not process to an on-failure destination (an SQS queue or SNS topic), so no event is lost.

choiceExplanations.0: This approach is unrelated to DynamoDB item changes and would only capture S3 object events, not the DynamoDB writes mentioned in the scenario, making it unsuitable for processing DynamoDB table modifications.
choiceExplanations.1: Manual reprocessing is not resilient or automated, lacks built-in retry mechanisms, and risks losing events if failures are not detected promptly, making it an unreliable approach for production workloads.
choiceExplanations.3: Scanning the entire table is inefficient, costly, and does not provide an ordered change log; it cannot reliably detect which items are new or modified, and lacks the automatic retry and failure handling capabilities of DynamoDB Streams.

resources.title: Retain discarded records for a DynamoDB event source in Lambda

question:
A fleet of EC2 instances across multiple AZs needs shared access to the same file system for user uploads. The application requires automatic high availability across AZs.
Which storage service is MOST suitable?
explanation: EFS is a managed, elastic NFS file system designed for shared access and is accessible from multiple AZs, supporting highly available shared storage for EC2/ECS workloads.

choiceExplanations.0: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is for long-term archives; objects must be restored before they can be read, which takes hours, and it is not a file system that instances can mount for active uploads.
choiceExplanations.1: This provides temporary block-level storage that is physically attached to the host and cannot be shared across instances or AZs, and data is lost when the instance stops or terminates.
choiceExplanations.2: EBS volumes attach to instances in a single Availability Zone only; Multi-Attach lets a few instances in that same AZ share a volume, but it cannot serve instances in different AZs.

resources.title: Attach an Amazon EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance

question:
A mobile app backend uses DynamoDB and must continue serving reads and writes even if an entire AWS Region becomes unavailable. The application requires near real-time replication between regions.
Which DynamoDB feature should you use?
choices: DynamoDB Streams only in a single region
explanation: Global tables provide multi-region, multi-active replication for DynamoDB, enabling reads and writes in multiple regions with near real-time replication and improved regional resilience.

choiceExplanations.0: DynamoDB Streams captures data modification events within a single table but does not provide cross-region replication by itself; it only operates within one region and cannot ensure availability if that region becomes unavailable.
choiceExplanations.1: Time to Live (TTL) is a feature that automatically deletes expired items from a table based on a timestamp attribute; it has no capability for cross-region replication or improving regional resilience.
choiceExplanations.2: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory caching service that improves read performance for DynamoDB tables within a single region; it does not provide multi-region replication or cross-region failover capabilities.

question:
A company wants to automatically scale a fleet of EC2 instances based on CPU utilization and replace unhealthy instances. They want the platform to handle capacity changes automatically.
Which solution best fits?
choices: Use an Application Load Balancer with a fixed number of instances
Use a single large EC2 instance with vertical scaling
Use an Auto Scaling group with scaling policies and health checks
Use EC2 Spot Instances only and manually add instances when needed
explanation: Auto Scaling groups provide automatic capacity management and instance replacement based on health checks and scaling policies, improving availability and resilience.

choiceExplanations.0: A load balancer only spreads traffic across the instances that already exist; with a fixed number of instances it cannot add capacity when CPU rises and it does not launch replacements for unhealthy instances.
choiceExplanations.1: Vertical scaling requires stopping the instance to change its size, causing downtime and not providing automatic scaling or health-based instance replacement; it also creates a single point of failure rather than a resilient fleet.
choiceExplanations.3: Manual scaling does not meet the requirement for automatic capacity management, and relying solely on Spot Instances without Auto Scaling means no automatic replacement of unhealthy or interrupted instances.

resources.title: Target tracking scaling policies for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

question:
A company needs to replicate objects from an S3 bucket in us-east-1 to another bucket in eu-west-1 for disaster recovery. Replication must be automatic after objects are uploaded.
Which feature should be used?
explanation: S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically replicates objects to a bucket in another region, supporting disaster recovery and compliance use cases.

choiceExplanations.0: This feature uploads large objects in parts to improve upload performance and reliability. It does not replicate objects between buckets or Regions.
choiceExplanations.2: This feature speeds up transfers to S3 by routing data through CloudFront edge locations. It does not automatically replicate objects to another Region.
choiceExplanations.3: This feature prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a retention period using a write-once-read-many model. It does not copy objects to another Region.

resources.title: Replicating objects within and across Regions
Amazon S3 Select is no longer available to new customers

question:
A multiplayer game uses UDP for real-time communication between clients and game servers running on EC2. The solution must distribute UDP traffic across instances with low latency.
Which load balancing option should you choose?
choices: Classic Load Balancer (CLB) with HTTP listeners
explanation: NLB operates at Layer 4 and supports UDP, providing very high performance and low latency load balancing. ALB is Layer 7 and supports HTTP/HTTPS, not UDP.

choiceExplanations.1: CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches and delivers web content from edge locations; it does not load balance raw UDP traffic across EC2 game servers.
choiceExplanations.2: CLB supports TCP and HTTP/HTTPS but does not support UDP traffic, making it unsuitable for real-time game communication requiring UDP.
choiceExplanations.3: ALB works at layer 7 for application traffic such as HTTP and HTTPS and has no UDP listener, so it cannot balance the game's UDP traffic.

resources.title: What is a Network Load Balancer?
What is an Application Load Balancer?

question:
A product catalog API requires single-digit millisecond latency for reads at very high request rates. The data is key-value and read-heavy.
Which AWS service is MOST suitable as the primary datastore?
explanation: DynamoDB is a managed key-value/NoSQL database designed for single-digit millisecond latency at scale. Relational and analytics services are not optimized for this access pattern.

choiceExplanations.0: Redshift is a data warehousing service optimized for complex analytical queries (OLAP) on large datasets, not for low-latency key-value lookups at high request rates typical of operational workloads.
choiceExplanations.2: RDS MySQL is a relational database that requires schema design and is not optimized for the simple key-value access patterns described; it also cannot match DynamoDB's consistent single-digit millisecond latency at very high request rates without significant scaling complexity.
choiceExplanations.3: Athena runs SQL queries over files in Amazon S3 and typically returns results in seconds, so it cannot give the single-digit millisecond reads a high-rate catalog API needs.

question:
A database on EC2 needs the highest possible IOPS with consistent, low-latency storage performance.
Which EBS volume type is MOST appropriate?
explanation: io1/io2 volumes are designed for high IOPS and consistent performance, which is critical for latency-sensitive databases.

choiceExplanations.0: Designed for infrequently accessed, cold data at the lowest cost, offering only 250 IOPS maximum and high latency, making it unsuitable for database workloads requiring high IOPS and low latency.
choiceExplanations.1: Optimized for large, sequential workloads like data warehouses and log processing where throughput (MB/s) matters more than IOPS, with a maximum of only 500 IOPS, which is inadequate for latency-sensitive database operations.
choiceExplanations.3: gp3 gives a 3,000 IOPS baseline and can be provisioned up to 80,000 IOPS, but io2 reaches far higher IOPS and is the type AWS recommends for latency-sensitive workloads, so gp3 is not the best answer for the highest possible IOPS.

resources.title: Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD volumes

question:
A client uploads very large files to S3, and uploads frequently fail due to unstable connections. They want higher reliability and better throughput.
Which S3 feature should they use?
explanation: Multipart Upload splits large objects into parts that can be uploaded in parallel and retried independently, improving throughput and reliability for large uploads.

choiceExplanations.1: This feature prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a specified retention period (WORM model), which is used for compliance and data protection, not for improving upload reliability or throughput.
choiceExplanations.2: S3 Inventory generates reports about objects and their metadata in a bucket on a scheduled basis, which is useful for auditing and management purposes, but does not address upload reliability or performance issues.
choiceExplanations.3: This feature enables hosting static web content directly from an S3 bucket, allowing public access to HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, but has no relation to improving upload reliability or throughput for large files.

resources.title: Uploading and copying objects using multipart upload in Amazon S3

question:
An application has read-heavy traffic and uses an Amazon RDS database. The team wants to increase read throughput without changing the application’s write logic.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Increase storage size to improve reads
Add one or more RDS read replicas and direct read traffic to them
Turn on a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and send reads to its standby
explanation: Read replicas scale out read traffic. In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment the standby exists for failover and cannot serve reads.

choiceExplanations.0: Increasing storage size does not improve read throughput; storage size affects capacity and potentially IOPS for certain storage types, but does not scale out read operations or reduce load on the primary database instance.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon S3 is an object storage service, not a relational database, and cannot replace RDS for transactional database workloads requiring SQL queries, ACID compliance, and relational data structures.
choiceExplanations.3: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment the standby is a synchronous replica kept only for failover, and it cannot be used to serve read traffic.

resources.title: Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS

question:
A company has a global user base accessing a latency-sensitive API hosted behind an ALB in a single region. They want improved global performance without changing the application.
Which service can provide faster global routing to the regional endpoint?
explanation: Global Accelerator uses the AWS global network to route users to the optimal endpoint, improving performance for latency-sensitive applications.

choiceExplanations.0: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers to and from Amazon S3 buckets through edge locations; it does not accelerate traffic to an API behind an Application Load Balancer.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private connection between an on-premises network and AWS; it does not improve the internet path of global users reaching a Region.
choiceExplanations.3: Geolocation routing answers DNS queries according to the user's location, but users still reach the single Region over the public internet, so it does not make the routing itself faster.

question:
A web application repeatedly queries the same small set of product data, causing high load on the database. The team wants sub-millisecond retrieval for hot items.
Which solution should they implement?
choices: Add read replicas to the database
Add an in-memory cache layer with Amazon ElastiCache
Move the hot items to Amazon S3
explanation: An in-memory cache like ElastiCache serves frequently read items from memory, which cuts database load and gives very low-latency retrieval for hot data.

choiceExplanations.0: Read replicas offload reads from the primary, but they are still database engines reading from storage, so they do not give the in-memory, sub-millisecond retrieval the team wants.
choiceExplanations.2: A larger instance can absorb more queries but still reads through the database engine, so it does not give in-memory sub-millisecond retrieval and raises cost.
choiceExplanations.3: S3 is object storage and is not designed for sub-millisecond lookups of hot items, and it would require changing how the application reads its data.

resources.title: Comparing node-based Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS clusters

question:
A containerized service needs to scale horizontally based on request rate, and tasks should be distributed across multiple AZs. The team prefers a managed container platform.
Which AWS service is MOST appropriate?
choices: Amazon ECS with Service Auto Scaling
explanation: ECS provides managed container orchestration, supports multi-AZ placement, and can scale services automatically based on metrics such as request count or CPU.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Batch queues and runs containerized batch jobs; it is not meant for an always-on service that scales horizontally with request rate.
choiceExplanations.2: Amazon ECR is a registry that stores container images; it does not run containers or scale a service.
choiceExplanations.3: This is a hybrid cloud storage service that connects on-premises environments to AWS cloud storage, providing file, volume, or tape gateway functionality, not a container management or orchestration service.

question:
A high-performance computing job requires low-latency, high-throughput network communication between EC2 instances.
Which EC2 placement strategy best supports this?
explanation: Cluster placement groups place instances close together within an AZ to achieve low-latency, high-throughput networking, suitable for tightly coupled workloads.

choiceExplanations.0: Instances in different Regions are far apart, so network latency is much higher than within one Availability Zone and they cannot be packed onto one network segment, the opposite of what a tightly coupled HPC job needs.
choiceExplanations.2: Spread placement groups put each instance on distinct hardware to limit correlated failures; they do not pack instances close together, so they give no low-latency advantage.
choiceExplanations.3: Partition placement groups split instances across partitions on separate racks for fault isolation in large distributed systems such as HDFS or Cassandra; they are not tuned for the lowest-latency, highest-throughput networking between instances.

resources.title: Placement strategies for your placement groups

question:
A company uploads files to S3 from users around the world and wants faster uploads by optimizing transfer paths to S3.
Which S3 feature can help?
explanation: Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations to accelerate uploads to S3 over long distances, improving performance for global users.

choiceExplanations.0: This feature prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a retention period using a write-once-read-many model. It does not improve upload speeds.
choiceExplanations.2: This is a low-cost storage class for long-term archives whose retrievals take many hours. It stores data; it does not speed up uploads.
choiceExplanations.3: This feature runs large-scale operations such as copying, tagging or invoking Lambda functions on existing S3 objects. It does not accelerate uploads of new objects.

resources.title: Configuring fast, secure file transfers using Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration

question:
A workload in private subnets calls Amazon S3 frequently. Using a NAT Gateway is generating significant data processing charges.
Which change reduces cost while keeping traffic private?
choices: Use AWS Direct Connect for internet access
Add another NAT Gateway in a second AZ
Add an S3 Gateway VPC endpoint and route S3 traffic through it
Move the instances to public subnets with public IPs
explanation: Gateway endpoints for S3 keep traffic within the AWS network and avoid NAT Gateway data processing charges for S3 access from private subnets.

choiceExplanations.0: Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity between on-premises networks and AWS. It is not used for VPC-to-S3 traffic and would add cost rather than reduce it.
choiceExplanations.1: A second NAT Gateway improves availability but does not reduce data processing charges; it adds another hourly charge and still processes the S3 traffic.
choiceExplanations.3: Putting the instances in public subnets with public IPs gives up the private design the stem requires and exposes them directly to the internet, instead of fixing the cost of sending S3 traffic through a NAT Gateway.

question:
A company wants to automatically move objects to cheaper storage classes over time without changing application code.
Which S3 feature supports this?
explanation: S3 Lifecycle rules move objects between storage classes, and can expire them, on a schedule, so no application code changes are needed.

choiceExplanations.0: This feature speeds up data transfers to S3 buckets over long distances using CloudFront edge locations. It does not move objects between storage classes.
choiceExplanations.2: This feature prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a retention period using a write-once-read-many model. It cannot transition objects between storage classes.
choiceExplanations.3: This feature sends a notification to a destination such as Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS or AWS Lambda when an event such as an object creation happens. It does not move objects between storage classes.

resources.title: Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle

question:
A company serves static files from S3 to users worldwide. They are paying high S3 data transfer costs and users in distant regions have high latency.
Which solution can both improve performance and potentially reduce origin load/cost?
choices: Use Glacier Deep Archive for static files
Move content from S3 to EBS
Use CloudFront in front of S3 to cache content at edge locations
Use a single larger EC2 instance as a file server
explanation: CloudFront edge caching reduces repeated origin fetches and improves latency for global users, which can also reduce S3 request load and overall cost depending on access patterns.

choiceExplanations.0: Glacier Deep Archive is designed for long-term archival storage with retrieval times of 12-48 hours, making it completely unsuitable for serving static files that users need to access immediately, and it would not reduce data transfer costs or improve latency.
choiceExplanations.1: EBS volumes are block storage attached to single EC2 instances in a specific Availability Zone, which would not improve global latency, would require managing EC2 infrastructure, and would likely increase costs compared to S3 while reducing availability and scalability.
choiceExplanations.3: A single EC2 instance in one region would not improve latency for users worldwide, introduces a single point of failure, requires infrastructure management, and would likely increase costs compared to using S3 with CloudFront.

resources.title: Manage how long content stays in the CloudFront cache (expiration)

question:
A company stores images in S3. A subset under the prefix /realtime/ must always have millisecond retrieval. Older images under /archive/ can take hours to retrieve after 90 days.
They want the most cost-effective lifecycle configuration.
Which option best meets the requirements?
choices: Lifecycle rule: keep /realtime/ in S3 Standard, and transition /archive/ to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days
Lifecycle rule: keep /realtime/ in S3 Standard, and transition /archive/ to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days
Use Intelligent-Tiering for all objects and never transition to archive tiers
Move the entire bucket to Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days
explanation: Prefix-based lifecycle rules let you keep the performance-critical prefix in a millisecond-access class while moving archival content to a cheaper archive class once retrieval time is allowed to be hours, which gives the lowest cost.

choiceExplanations.1: Standard-IA still gives millisecond access, but its storage price is higher than the Glacier classes. Because /archive/ can wait hours, an archive class is cheaper, so this is not the most cost-effective choice.
choiceExplanations.2: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between millisecond-access tiers automatically, but with the archive tiers left off it never reaches the lowest-cost storage that the /archive/ data could use.
choiceExplanations.3: Glacier Deep Archive objects must be restored first and take hours (up to about two days) to retrieve, so /realtime/ objects could not be served in milliseconds.

resources.title: Understanding S3 Glacier storage classes for long-term data storage
Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle

question:
A company uses AWS Organizations with multiple accounts. The security team mandates that no one can disable CloudTrail logging or delete CloudTrail log files, even in development accounts.
Developers still need broad permissions within their accounts for day-to-day work.
Which combination of controls best enforces this requirement?
choices: Place CloudTrail logs in each account’s local S3 bucket with bucket policies that allow deletion only by admins
Attach AdministratorAccess to all developers and rely on CloudTrail alarms to detect changes
Apply an SCP that denies stopping/deleting CloudTrail and denies deleting objects in the centralized log bucket; store logs in a dedicated logging account
Enable AWS Config in each account and automatically revert changes to CloudTrail via a Lambda function
explanation: SCPs provide account-level guardrails that apply even to administrators in member accounts. Centralizing CloudTrail logs in a dedicated logging account further reduces risk. Detective/auto-remediation is helpful but does not prevent the action from occurring.

choiceExplanations.0: Place CloudTrail logs in each account's local S3 bucket with bucket policies that allow deletion only by admins: This approach keeps logs in individual accounts where local administrators can modify bucket policies or assume admin roles to delete logs, and it does not prevent disabling CloudTrail itself since bucket policies only control S3 access, not CloudTrail configuration.
choiceExplanations.1: This is a detective control only, not preventive; alarms notify after the fact but do not prevent developers with AdministratorAccess from actually disabling CloudTrail or deleting logs, violating the requirement that no one can perform these actions.
choiceExplanations.3: This is a reactive/remediation approach that allows the prohibited action to occur temporarily before being reverted, creating a window where logging gaps exist; it also does not prevent log file deletion and the Lambda function itself could be disabled by account administrators.

question:
A company wants employees to sign in to AWS using their corporate identity provider (IdP) and be assigned AWS permissions based on their job role. The solution should avoid creating IAM users and should be easy to manage as employees join/leave.
Which approach is MOST suitable?
choices: Use Amazon Cognito user pools for employee access to the AWS console
Use access keys distributed through a password manager and rotate them monthly
Use AWS IAM Identity Center integrated with the corporate IdP and assign permission sets to users and groups
Create an IAM user for each employee and enforce MFA
explanation: IAM Identity Center is designed for workforce authentication and authorization into AWS accounts, integrating with external IdPs and mapping users/groups to permission sets. This avoids managing long-lived IAM users.

choiceExplanations.0: Amazon Cognito is designed for customer-facing application authentication (web/mobile apps), not for workforce access to the AWS Management Console or AWS account resources; IAM Identity Center is the appropriate service for employee workforce identity management.
choiceExplanations.1: Access keys are long-term credentials that require manual management and rotation, creating security risks and administrative overhead; this approach does not integrate with corporate IdPs and does not meet the requirement to avoid creating IAM users since access keys are associated with IAM users.
choiceExplanations.3: This directly contradicts the requirement to avoid creating IAM users and creates significant management overhead as employees join and leave the company, requiring manual user lifecycle management rather than leveraging the corporate IdP for centralized identity management.

question:
A company wants to detect and alert on suspicious root account usage (console sign-in or access key usage) in near real time. They also want a searchable history of these events.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Enable VPC Flow Logs and create alarms when port 443 traffic increases
Use AWS CloudTrail with an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches root user events and notifies an Amazon SNS topic, and keep the logs in Amazon S3 for search
Enable AWS Config and run compliance evaluations every 24 hours
Enable AWS Shield Advanced and monitor Shield events
explanation: Root account usage is captured in CloudTrail. EventBridge can match specific CloudTrail events and trigger near-real-time notifications. Centralized log storage enables audit and search.

choiceExplanations.0: VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic metadata (IP addresses, ports, protocols) at the VPC level, not user authentication or API activity. Root account sign-ins and API calls are identity-level events that occur outside VPC networking and cannot be detected through flow logs.
choiceExplanations.2: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes and compliance state, not user authentication events or API activity. Additionally, 24-hour evaluation intervals do not meet the near real-time alerting requirement specified in the question.
choiceExplanations.3: AWS Shield Advanced protects against DDoS attacks on AWS resources and does not monitor or detect IAM user activity, console sign-ins, or API calls. It is designed for network-layer protection, not identity and access monitoring.

question:
A company must encrypt EBS volumes on EC2 instances. The security team requires that the key be rotated automatically on a schedule the team controls, and that use of the key be limited to a specific set of roles through the key policy.
Which solution should you implement?
choices: Use client-side encryption inside the EC2 instance and store the keys in the AMI
Use unencrypted EBS volumes and enforce TLS for all disk I/O
Use EBS encryption with a customer managed KMS key, automatic rotation enabled and a key policy that names the approved roles
Use EBS encryption with the AWS managed key aws/ebs and control access with IAM policies only
explanation: Customer managed KMS keys support automatic rotation with a rotation period you choose and a key policy you write. EBS integrates directly with KMS for encryption at rest.

choiceExplanations.0: Storing encryption keys in an AMI is a security anti-pattern because AMIs can be shared or copied, exposing the keys. It also gives no automatic rotation and does not use KMS-backed EBS encryption.
choiceExplanations.1: TLS protects data in transit, not data at rest on a volume. Leaving the volumes unencrypted fails the requirement to encrypt them.
choiceExplanations.3: The AWS managed key aws/ebs is rotated automatically every year, but the schedule cannot be changed, and its key policy cannot be edited, so the team cannot limit use of the key through the key policy.

question:
A microservice running on ECS retrieves DB credentials from Secrets Manager. A new compliance rule requires that services must not access secrets unless they are running in the approved VPC and use a specific VPC endpoint.
Which design best meets this requirement?
choices: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager, and attach a secret resource policy that denies access unless the request comes through that endpoint (aws:SourceVpce)
Use environment variables and rotate the container image on every rotation
Store the secret in an S3 bucket and restrict access with a bucket policy
Use a NAT Gateway and allow the service to call Secrets Manager over the internet
explanation: An interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) gives the VPC a private path to Secrets Manager, and a Deny statement with the aws:SourceVpce condition in the secret's resource policy rejects requests that do not arrive through that endpoint.

choiceExplanations.1: Environment variables expose secrets in plaintext within the container configuration, which is a security anti-pattern, and requiring container image rebuilds for credential rotation is operationally inefficient and does not enforce VPC endpoint access requirements.
choiceExplanations.2: This abandons Secrets Manager entirely, losing its automatic rotation, encryption, and auditing capabilities, and S3 bucket policies alone cannot enforce that access must occur through a specific VPC endpoint for Secrets Manager as required.
choiceExplanations.3: This routes traffic over the public internet rather than through a private VPC endpoint, directly violating the compliance requirement that secrets must only be accessed through the approved VPC using a specific VPC endpoint.

resources.title: Resource-based policies (AWS Secrets Manager User Guide)

question:
A company exposes private documents to authenticated customers via CloudFront. Documents must remain private in S3, and direct access to the S3 bucket must be blocked.
Which architecture should you implement?
choices: Make the S3 bucket public and rely on signed URLs to hide the object keys
Expose the S3 bucket to customers through an internet-facing Application Load Balancer
Use S3 static website hosting with Basic Auth enabled on the website endpoint
Use CloudFront with Origin Access Control on the S3 origin, and signed URLs or signed cookies for viewers
explanation: Origin Access Control lets only the CloudFront distribution read the private S3 origin, so direct access to the bucket is blocked. Signed URLs or signed cookies then limit which viewers can fetch the documents through CloudFront.

choiceExplanations.0: A public bucket violates the requirement that documents stay private in S3. Anyone who learns or guesses an object key can read the object directly, and signed URLs only apply to CloudFront, not to a public S3 endpoint.
choiceExplanations.1: An Application Load Balancer forwards to EC2 instances, IP addresses or Lambda functions, not to an S3 bucket, so this design cannot work.
choiceExplanations.2: The S3 static website endpoint only serves publicly readable content and has no Basic Auth feature, so it cannot keep documents private or block direct access.

resources.title: Restrict access to an Amazon S3 origin

question:
A company wants a centralized view of security findings across GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config rules for all AWS accounts. They also want to automatically open tickets when critical findings appear.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Enable CloudWatch Logs Insights across accounts and query the logs for security events on a schedule
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor in every account and export its security checks to a weekly report
Enable Amazon GuardDuty in every account and review the findings in each account's console
Use AWS Security Hub with a delegated administrator account and route critical findings through EventBridge rules to a ticketing workflow
explanation: Security Hub aggregates findings from multiple AWS services and can centralize them in a delegated administrator account. EventBridge can trigger automated workflows based on finding severity.

choiceExplanations.0: CloudWatch Logs Insights is designed for querying and analyzing log data, not for aggregating security findings from services like GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config rules. It lacks native integration with these security services and does not provide a unified security findings dashboard or automated ticketing capabilities.
choiceExplanations.1: Trusted Advisor provides best practice recommendations for cost optimization, performance, security, and fault tolerance, but it does not aggregate findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, or Config rules. Weekly manual exports do not meet the requirement for automatic ticket creation when critical findings appear.
choiceExplanations.2: GuardDuty is a threat detection service and only one source of findings. Reviewing it account by account gives no single view across accounts, no Inspector or Config findings, and no automatic ticket creation.

resources.title: AWS service integrations with Security Hub CSPM

question:
An application in Account A needs to write objects to an S3 bucket in Account B. The security team requires least privilege, no long-lived credentials, and clear separation of duties.
Which option best meets these requirements?
choices: Create an IAM role in Account B that Account A can assume, grant it s3:PutObject to the bucket, and allow the role in the bucket policy
Use pre-signed URLs generated by Account A without changing Account B
Create an IAM user in Account B and share the access keys with Account A
Make the bucket public-write and use object prefixes to separate writes
explanation: Cross-account role assumption provides temporary credentials and supports least privilege. Bucket policies can restrict writes to the role, avoiding shared long-lived access keys.

choiceExplanations.1: Pre-signed URLs can only grant permissions that the signing entity already has; Account A cannot generate valid pre-signed URLs for Account B's bucket without first being granted cross-account access through bucket policies or IAM roles.
choiceExplanations.2: This approach uses long-lived credentials (access keys), which directly violates the requirement for no long-lived credentials and introduces security risks from credential sharing between accounts.
choiceExplanations.3: Public-write access violates least privilege principles by allowing anyone on the internet to write to the bucket, creating severe security risks and failing to provide clear separation of duties or access control.

resources.title: Cross account resource access in IAM

question:
A team uses IAM roles for EC2 instances. During an incident, a developer added a broad inline policy to the instance role. Security wants to ensure that role permissions cannot be expanded beyond a predefined maximum, but still allow adding narrower permissions when needed.
Which control should be used?
choices: Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the EC2 instance
Attach a permissions boundary to the role to cap its maximum permissions
Use an ACL on the EC2 instance to deny outbound network traffic
Add the role to an IAM group with restricted permissions
explanation: Permissions boundaries can be applied to roles (not just users) to limit the maximum effective permissions, preventing expansion beyond a defined scope while still allowing additional allowed permissions to be attached.

choiceExplanations.0: AWS Shield Advanced is a DDoS protection service that safeguards against distributed denial-of-service attacks, not an IAM permission control mechanism, so it has no effect on limiting role permissions.
choiceExplanations.2: Network ACLs control network traffic flow at the subnet level and have no relationship to IAM permissions; blocking network traffic does not prevent a role from having expanded IAM permissions.
choiceExplanations.3: IAM roles cannot be added to IAM groups; groups are only for IAM users, making this option technically impossible and irrelevant to controlling role permissions.

question:
A company requires that all S3 access to a sensitive bucket must come from within their VPC over a specific VPC endpoint, and any request from the public internet must be denied, even if credentials are valid.
Which solution best enforces this?
choices: Enable SSE-KMS on the bucket and add a key policy statement that denies kms:Decrypt to requests coming from the internet
Add a bucket policy that denies every request that does not arrive through the VPC endpoint (aws:sourceVpce), and create an S3 gateway VPC endpoint
Turn on S3 Block Public Access for the account and the bucket, and leave the bucket policy unchanged
Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket so that all requests are forced through edge locations
explanation: A bucket policy with a Deny statement on requests that do not come through the named VPC endpoint (aws:sourceVpce) rejects every other path, even for valid credentials. The S3 gateway endpoint gives the VPC a private route to the bucket.

choiceExplanations.0: SSE-KMS protects the object contents and controls who can decrypt, but it does not control the network path. Requests such as listing or deleting objects need no kms:Decrypt, and a key policy cannot simply deny 'the internet'.
choiceExplanations.2: Block Public Access stops anonymous and public access, but it does not stop authenticated requests from outside the VPC, so valid credentials still work from the internet.
choiceExplanations.3: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers through CloudFront edge locations. It does not restrict the network path, and requests still come from the public internet.

resources.title: Controlling access from VPC endpoints with bucket policies

question:
A financial services company runs an internet-facing application behind CloudFront and ALB. They are concerned about large-scale DDoS attacks and want DDoS response support plus cost protection for scaling-related charges during an attack.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Rely on AWS Shield Standard and tighten the security groups on the ALB and the origin instances
Use AWS WAF with rate-based rules on the CloudFront distribution and the ALB, without subscribing to Shield Advanced
Use Amazon GuardDuty to detect DDoS attempts and notify the security team so it can respond manually
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, add the CloudFront distribution and the ALB as protected resources, and attach an AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule
explanation: Shield Advanced adds access to the DDoS response team and cost protection (service credits for DDoS-related scaling charges) for the resources it protects. For CloudFront and ALB, the protected resources need an AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule, which also filters application-layer traffic.

choiceExplanations.0: Shield Standard provides basic DDoS protection automatically at no cost but does not include DDoS response team access or cost protection for scaling charges during attacks, which are key requirements stated in the question. Security groups do not stop volumetric attacks.
choiceExplanations.1: AWS WAF rate-based rules help against application-layer floods, but WAF alone does not give access to the DDoS response team or credits for scaling charges; those are Shield Advanced benefits.
choiceExplanations.2: GuardDuty is a threat detection service that raises findings; it does not mitigate DDoS attacks, give access to a response team, or protect against attack-driven charges.

resources.title: Requesting a credit in AWS Shield Advanced after an attack

question:
A company uses KMS keys for encrypting data. Security requires that only a specific microservice role can decrypt data, and administrators should be able to manage the key (rotate/disable) but not decrypt application data.
Which configuration best meets this requirement?
choices: Use a customer-managed KMS key with a key policy that separates key administration permissions from key usage (encrypt/decrypt) permissions
Use an AWS-managed KMS key and attach decrypt permissions to the admin role
Use S3 SSE-S3 so KMS policies are not needed
Store the key material in the application container and restrict access with security groups
explanation: KMS key policies can separate administrative actions (like enabling/disabling, rotating) from cryptographic usage actions (Encrypt/Decrypt). Grant decrypt only to the microservice role while allowing admins to administer the key without data access.

choiceExplanations.1: AWS-managed KMS keys do not allow modification of their key policies, so you cannot customize permissions to separate administrative actions from cryptographic usage. Additionally, this choice incorrectly grants decrypt permissions to admins, which violates the requirement that administrators should not be able to decrypt application data.
choiceExplanations.2: SSE-S3 uses Amazon S3-managed keys where AWS controls all key management, providing no ability to define granular access controls or separate administrative and usage permissions. This approach offers no mechanism to restrict decryption to only a specific microservice role.
choiceExplanations.3: Storing encryption keys directly in application containers is a security anti-pattern that violates AWS best practices for key management. Security groups operate at the network layer and cannot control access to data or encryption keys within a container, and this approach lacks the audit, rotation, and access control capabilities provided by KMS.

question:
A company must prove that security groups never allow inbound 0.0.0.0/0 access to SSH or RDP, and they need continuous monitoring with automatic evidence for auditors.
Which solution best meets these requirements?
choices: Use AWS Config managed rules to evaluate security groups continuously and keep the compliance history
Enable Amazon GuardDuty and rely on its findings for open ports
Use Amazon VPC Flow Logs and manually inspect the logs for port 22 and 3389 traffic
Use AWS CloudTrail only and search for AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress calls
explanation: AWS Config continuously evaluates resource configurations against rules and retains compliance history, which is useful for audit evidence. CloudTrail and flow logs are helpful but do not provide continuous configuration compliance evaluation by themselves.

choiceExplanations.1: GuardDuty is a threat detection service that analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events for malicious activity, but it does not continuously evaluate security group configurations against compliance rules or provide the configuration compliance history needed for audit evidence.
choiceExplanations.2: VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic metadata but do not evaluate security group configurations; they only show actual traffic that occurred, require manual inspection which is not continuous monitoring, and do not provide automatic compliance evidence for auditors.
choiceExplanations.3: CloudTrail logs API calls and can show when security group rules were modified, but it does not continuously evaluate the current state of security group configurations against compliance rules or automatically generate compliance reports for auditors.

question:
A SaaS provider runs its primary workload in Region A. The application stack includes ALB + EC2, an RDS database, and an S3 bucket for user uploads. The business requires:
- RPO of 15 minutes for the database
- RTO of 1 hour for the application
- Minimal ongoing costs in the secondary region
Which disaster recovery strategy BEST meets these requirements?
choices: Warm standby: run a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the stack in Region B at all times
Backup and restore only: keep no resources in Region B and rely solely on nightly backups
Active-active: run the full stack at production scale in both regions at all times
Pilot light: replicate the database to Region B, keep the rest of the stack switched off, and start and scale it up on failover
explanation: Pilot light keeps only the replicated core (the database) running in the secondary Region, which costs less than warm standby or active-active while recovering faster than backup and restore. Continuous or frequent cross-Region replication supports the 15-minute RPO, and starting and scaling up the rest of the stack fits within the 1-hour RTO.

choiceExplanations.0: Warm standby would meet the 15-minute RPO and the 1-hour RTO, but it keeps a running copy of the whole stack in Region B at all times, which costs more than a pilot light and conflicts with the requirement for minimal ongoing cost.
choiceExplanations.1: Nightly backups cannot achieve a 15-minute RPO since data loss could be up to 24 hours, and restoring an entire infrastructure from scratch would likely exceed the 1-hour RTO requirement due to the time needed to provision and configure all resources.
choiceExplanations.2: This approach provides the best RTO and RPO but completely violates the minimal ongoing costs requirement, as it doubles infrastructure costs by running full production capacity in both regions simultaneously.

resources.title: Disaster recovery options in the cloud

question:
A company runs an Aurora MySQL cluster for a critical application. They want protection against an AZ failure with automatic failover, and they also want to be able to fail over to another region for a regional outage with the lowest RPO possible.
Which design is MOST appropriate?
choices: Use a single-instance Aurora cluster and take manual snapshots to copy to another region
Use DynamoDB global tables instead of Aurora without changing the application
Use Aurora Multi-AZ (cluster with replicas in multiple AZs) and configure Aurora Global Database for cross-region replication
Use RDS read replicas in the same AZ only and promote one manually
explanation: Aurora provides Multi-AZ high availability via replicas and automatic failover within a region. Aurora Global Database provides low-latency cross-region replication to reduce RPO for regional failover scenarios.

choiceExplanations.0: A single-instance cluster provides no automatic failover protection against AZ failure, and manual snapshot copies lose all changes since the last copy, a far higher RPO than Aurora Global Database, which typically replicates with latency under a second.
choiceExplanations.1: Switching from Aurora MySQL to DynamoDB would require significant application changes since DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value database with a completely different data model and API than a relational MySQL database.
choiceExplanations.3: This provides no AZ failure protection since all replicas are in the same AZ, requires manual promotion instead of automatic failover, and provides no cross-region disaster recovery capability for regional outages.

question:
A company processes orders using SQS and Lambda. The same order event can be delivered more than once due to retries, and the downstream system must never create duplicate orders.
The team wants a resilient design that handles retries safely.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Use SNS only without SQS so delivery happens once
Make the Lambda processing idempotent using a DynamoDB table to track processed order IDs, and keep retries/DLQ for failures
Increase the SQS visibility timeout to 12 hours so duplicates cannot occur
Disable retries in Lambda so messages are never reprocessed
explanation: Event-driven systems can deliver duplicates. Idempotent processing (tracking processed IDs in DynamoDB or equivalent) ensures retries do not create duplicates, while DLQs capture poison messages for investigation.

choiceExplanations.0: SNS also provides at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once, so duplicates can still occur. Additionally, removing SQS eliminates important benefits like message buffering, retry handling, and dead-letter queue capabilities for failed messages.
choiceExplanations.2: Visibility timeout only prevents other consumers from receiving a message while it's being processed; it does not prevent SQS's inherent at-least-once delivery behavior where the same message can be delivered multiple times. This approach also creates operational issues if processing fails.
choiceExplanations.3: Disabling retries would cause messages to be lost if transient failures occur, reducing system resilience. This approach sacrifices reliability and does not address the fundamental issue that SQS standard queues can deliver the same message more than once regardless of Lambda retry settings.

question:
A production service runs on ECS Fargate behind an ALB. During deployments, users occasionally see 5xx errors because tasks are terminated before the new tasks are ready.
The team wants zero-downtime deployments with minimal effort.
Which approach should they implement?
choices: Switch to an NLB because it does not do health checks
Use an ECS service with rolling updates, configure ALB health checks, and set a deployment minimumHealthyPercent/maximumPercent so new tasks pass health checks before old tasks are drained
Place CloudFront in front of the ALB and disable origin health checks
Manually stop all running tasks, then start new tasks after the image is updated
explanation: ECS service deployments can be configured to keep a minimum healthy capacity while starting new tasks. Combined with ALB health checks and connection draining, this avoids terminating old tasks until new ones are healthy.

choiceExplanations.0: This is factually incorrect as NLB does perform health checks on targets. Additionally, switching load balancer types does not address the core deployment issue of tasks being terminated before new ones are ready, and removing health checks would actually make the problem worse by routing traffic to unhealthy targets.
choiceExplanations.2: CloudFront caching cannot prevent 5xx errors during deployments when backend tasks are unavailable, and disabling health checks does not solve the underlying issue of task termination timing. This adds unnecessary complexity without addressing the deployment coordination problem.
choiceExplanations.3: This approach guarantees downtime because there is a gap between stopping old tasks and new tasks becoming healthy. It also requires manual effort, which contradicts the requirement for minimal effort and does not provide zero-downtime deployments.

resources.title: Deploy Amazon ECS services by replacing tasks

question:
A company has two copies of a web application: one in us-east-1 and one in eu-west-1. They want active-active traffic distribution, but if one region fails, 100% of traffic should go to the healthy region automatically.
Which Route 53 configuration best meets this?
choices: Use geolocation routing without health checks
Use failover routing with us-east-1 as primary and eu-west-1 as secondary
Use simple routing with both endpoints in a single record
Use weighted routing with health checks on each regional endpoint
explanation: Weighted routing can split traffic across multiple endpoints and, when paired with health checks, will stop returning unhealthy endpoints—effectively shifting traffic to the healthy region automatically.

choiceExplanations.0: Geolocation routing directs traffic based on user location, not for active-active distribution, and without health checks Route 53 cannot detect regional failures or automatically redirect traffic to the healthy region.
choiceExplanations.1: Failover routing is active-passive: all traffic goes to the primary while it is healthy, so it does not give the active-active distribution the company wants.
choiceExplanations.2: Simple routing cannot be associated with health checks, so Route 53 keeps returning the failed Region's endpoint and clients may be sent to it.

question:
A company replicates data using S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR). They recently enabled CRR but noticed that older objects that already existed in the bucket were not replicated.
They want all existing objects to be replicated to the destination bucket.
Which action should they take?
choices: Disable and re-enable the replication rule so that it backfills all existing objects automatically
Run an S3 Batch Replication job to replicate the existing objects, because a replication rule applies only to objects added after it is enabled
Create a second replication rule with an empty filter so that it also matches the objects already in the bucket
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to speed up replication of existing objects
explanation: Live replication only copies objects that are created after the rule is enabled. S3 Batch Replication is the on-demand job that replicates objects that existed before the rule, were replicated before, or failed replication.

choiceExplanations.0: Turning the rule off and on does not backfill anything; a replication rule only applies to objects created after it is in effect.
choiceExplanations.2: A new rule, even with an empty filter, is still live replication and applies only to new objects, so the existing objects stay unreplicated.
choiceExplanations.3: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance uploads and downloads. It does not replicate objects or change which objects a replication rule covers.

resources.title: Replicating existing objects with Batch Replication

question:
An application stores user session state in-memory on the web servers. During Auto Scaling events, users are frequently logged out because they land on new instances.
The company needs a resilient approach that preserves sessions even when instances scale in/out or fail.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Enable ALB sticky sessions and store sessions only in instance memory
Increase the Auto Scaling cooldown to reduce scaling events
Store sessions in a centralized store such as Amazon ElastiCache instead of on-instance memory
Use a larger instance type so scaling isn't needed
explanation: Keeping session state in a shared store such as Amazon ElastiCache (or DynamoDB) outside the web servers lets any instance serve any user, so scaling in, scaling out or an instance failure no longer logs people out. Sticky sessions only pin a user to one instance, and the session is lost when that instance is deregistered or becomes unhealthy.

choiceExplanations.0: While sticky sessions route users to the same instance, sessions are still lost when that instance terminates during scale-in events or fails, making this approach not resilient to instance failures or scaling activities.
choiceExplanations.1: This only delays scaling events rather than solving the fundamental problem; sessions will still be lost when scaling eventually occurs, and it reduces the application's ability to respond to demand changes effectively.
choiceExplanations.3: This approach is not resilient because a single larger instance creates a single point of failure, and it does not address the core issue of session state being tied to instance memory rather than being externalized.

resources.title: Edit target group attributes for your Application Load Balancer
Common ElastiCache Use Cases and How ElastiCache Can Help

question:
A critical internal service runs on EC2 instances in a single subnet in one AZ. The business requires the service to remain available during an AZ outage.
Which change provides the MOST reliable improvement?
choices: Enable detailed monitoring and add an alarm that restarts the instance if it fails
Run the service in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer, with subnets in at least two Availability Zones
Move the service to a larger instance type in the same Availability Zone
Take hourly EBS snapshots and restore them in another Availability Zone if the zone fails
explanation: High availability against AZ failure requires running across multiple AZs. An ASG plus a load balancer and subnets in multiple AZs ensures the service can continue even if one AZ becomes unavailable.

choiceExplanations.0: Detailed monitoring and a restart alarm only help when an instance fails inside a healthy Availability Zone; if the whole zone is unavailable there is nowhere to restart it, so the service stays down.
choiceExplanations.2: A larger instance adds compute capacity but remains in the same Availability Zone, so an outage of that zone still takes the service down.
choiceExplanations.3: Snapshots protect the data, but restoring them in another zone after an outage means building new instances by hand and accepting downtime, so the service is not available during the outage.

resources.title: Resilience in Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling

question:
A company uses an RDS MySQL database. Reporting queries occasionally cause performance issues for the production workload.
They want to isolate reporting reads without impacting write performance and still keep production highly available.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Scale up the primary database instance and run reporting on it
Create an RDS read replica for reporting queries, and keep Multi-AZ enabled for the primary for availability
Enable a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and direct reporting queries to the standby instance
Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster in front of the database and run the reporting queries on the cache
explanation: Read replicas offload read-heavy workloads like reporting, while Multi-AZ protects availability. The standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment exists only for failover and cannot serve read traffic.

choiceExplanations.0: Scaling up increases capacity but does not isolate reporting queries from production workloads, meaning reporting queries would still compete for resources with production writes and could impact performance.
choiceExplanations.2: The standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment exists solely for automatic failover and cannot be queried, so the reporting queries would have nowhere to run.
choiceExplanations.3: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache for repeated lookups; it cannot run ad hoc relational reporting queries, so the reporting load would still land on the production database.

resources.title: Multi-AZ DB instance deployments for Amazon RDS

question:
A company uses Amazon DynamoDB with provisioned capacity. During sudden, unpredictable traffic spikes, requests are throttled and the application returns errors. Traffic is low the rest of the time, and the company does not want to pay for capacity it rarely uses.
Which configuration is MOST appropriate?
choices: Raise the provisioned capacity to the expected peak and leave it there
Keep the provisioned capacity and turn on DynamoDB Streams
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode
Keep the provisioned capacity and add more retries in the application
explanation: On-demand capacity mode scales with the traffic automatically and charges per request, so it absorbs steep, unpredictable spikes without a fixed throughput limit and costs little when traffic is low. Provisioned capacity with auto scaling fits traffic that follows a pattern you can predict.

choiceExplanations.0: Provisioning for the peak at all times would stop the throttling but means paying for unused capacity during the quiet periods, which the company wants to avoid.
choiceExplanations.1: DynamoDB Streams records item-level changes for downstream processing. It adds no read or write throughput, so throttling would continue.
choiceExplanations.3: Retries repeat requests against the same throughput limit. They do not add capacity, so the spikes would still be throttled.

resources.title: Evaluate your DynamoDB table's auto scaling settings

question:
A company wants to decouple multiple microservices and route events based on event content (for example, route “fraud-alert” events to a specific service and “order-created” events to another).
They also want built-in retry and DLQ capabilities.
Which service is MOST suitable?
choices: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks
Amazon EventBridge with rules and targets (plus DLQ where appropriate)
explanation: EventBridge supports content-based routing using rules and can integrate with targets that provide retry/DLQ behavior, enabling resilient event-driven architectures across services.

choiceExplanations.0: S3 event notifications are limited to triggering on S3 bucket events (like object creation or deletion) and cannot perform content-based routing on custom event types like 'fraud-alert' or 'order-created' from microservices, nor do they provide built-in DLQ capabilities.
choiceExplanations.1: Lifecycle hooks are specifically designed to pause Auto Scaling actions during instance launch or termination to perform custom actions, not for general-purpose event routing between microservices or content-based message filtering.
choiceExplanations.2: Route 53 Resolver is a DNS service that handles DNS queries between on-premises networks and AWS VPCs, and has no capability for application event routing, message queuing, or dead-letter queue functionality.

question:
A company wants strong protection against accidental deletions and ransomware for an S3 bucket, while still being able to recover data to a previous point in time.
They also need the ability to replicate data to another region for DR.
Which combination best meets these requirements?
choices: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and store objects as multipart uploads
Use S3 static website hosting and enable logging
Enable S3 versioning with MFA Delete, and use Same-Region Replication to copy objects to a second bucket in the same Region
Enable S3 versioning and S3 Object Lock, and configure Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in a second Region
explanation: Versioning lets the company restore a previous version after a deletion or overwrite, and Object Lock stops ransomware or users from deleting or changing protected versions. Cross-Region Replication adds a copy in another Region for disaster recovery.

choiceExplanations.0: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers and multipart upload handles large files; neither protects against deletion or ransomware, supports point-in-time recovery, or replicates to another Region.
choiceExplanations.1: Static website hosting serves web content and logging only records requests. Neither protects data, restores earlier versions or copies data to another Region.
choiceExplanations.2: MFA Delete and a copy in the same Region add some protection, but Same-Region Replication keeps the copy in the same Region, so it does not meet the requirement to replicate to another Region for disaster recovery, and it lacks Object Lock's protection against ransomware.

resources.title: Replicating encrypted objects (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C)

question:
A company uses CloudFront in front of an ALB. The origin sometimes becomes temporarily overloaded, and the company wants CloudFront to serve stale cached objects during brief origin outages to improve resilience.
Which approach achieves this?
choices: Have the origin send Cache-Control headers that include the stale-if-error directive
Use Route 53 weighted routing between two CloudFront distributions
Increase the origin response timeout so CloudFront waits longer for the overloaded ALB
Disable caching entirely so CloudFront always fetches from the origin
explanation: The stale-if-error Cache-Control directive tells CloudFront to keep serving an expired cached object when the origin is unreachable or returns an error, for the time the directive specifies (never beyond the maximum TTL).

choiceExplanations.1: Weighted routing splits traffic between two distributions, but both would still depend on the same overloaded ALB and neither serves stale objects.
choiceExplanations.2: A longer origin response timeout makes CloudFront wait longer for a slow origin; it does not make CloudFront serve a cached copy when the origin fails.
choiceExplanations.3: Turning caching off sends every request to the origin, which makes the overload worse and removes any cached copy to serve.

resources.title: Determining how long content stays in the cache (expiration): serve stale content

question:
A company has a multi-step serverless workflow (validate → charge → provision → notify). They need reliable orchestration with retries, error handling, and the ability to see where executions failed.
Which service is MOST suitable?
explanation: Step Functions provides workflow orchestration with built-in retries, error handling, state tracking, and execution history, improving resilience and observability for multi-step serverless processes.

choiceExplanations.0: S3 is an object storage service designed for storing and retrieving data, not for orchestrating workflows; it lacks built-in capabilities for workflow coordination, retries, error handling, or execution state tracking.
choiceExplanations.2: SNS is a pub/sub messaging service for sending notifications and decoupling components, but it cannot orchestrate multi-step workflows, manage execution state, implement retry logic, or provide visibility into where failures occurred in a process.
choiceExplanations.3: Glue is a managed ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) service designed for data integration and preparation tasks, not for general-purpose serverless workflow orchestration; it lacks the flexible state machine capabilities, custom retry policies, and execution visualization needed for this use case.

resources.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows

question:
An application receives sudden bursts of work that can be processed asynchronously. The workers run in an Auto Scaling group, but scaling out takes several minutes because of long bootstrapping, which causes errors during bursts.
The team wants a more resilient way to absorb short spikes while the group scales out.
Which solution is MOST suitable?
choices: Increase the instance size so scale-out is unnecessary
Place an Amazon SQS queue between the request intake and the workers so the backlog waits while workers scale out and drain it
Disable health checks to avoid replacing instances
Move the application to a single larger EC2 instance
explanation: Introducing a queue buffers bursty workloads and decouples ingestion from processing. This helps maintain resilience during spikes while compute capacity scales to handle the backlog.

choiceExplanations.0: Vertical scaling alone cannot handle unlimited traffic bursts and still has finite capacity limits; it does not address the fundamental problem of absorbing sudden spikes and introduces a single point of failure without providing elasticity.
choiceExplanations.2: This does not address the scaling latency problem and would actually reduce resilience by allowing unhealthy instances to remain in service, potentially causing more errors rather than fewer during traffic bursts.
choiceExplanations.3: This eliminates Auto Scaling entirely, creates a single point of failure, and still has finite capacity that cannot handle unpredictable traffic bursts regardless of instance size.

resources.title: Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS
Decrease latency for applications with long boot times using warm pools

question:
A global news website serves dynamic HTML (personalized) and large static images from the same domain. Users complain that pages are slow during peak hours.
Requirements:
- Personalized HTML must not be cached for long
- Images should be cached globally to reduce origin load
- Minimal application code changes
Which solution BEST meets these requirements?
choices: Use an NLB in front of the web servers to cache HTML
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration for the images and keep serving the HTML from the origin
Use CloudFront with separate cache behaviors by path: cache the images for a long time and cache the personalized HTML for little or no time
Increase the origin server instance size and disable caching
explanation: CloudFront cache behaviors allow different caching rules per path pattern. You can cache static assets heavily while keeping personalized content minimally cached and forwarding only what is required, improving performance and reducing origin load with limited code changes.

choiceExplanations.0: A Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and distributes traffic; it has no caching capability.
choiceExplanations.1: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers to and from an S3 bucket over the AWS edge network but does not cache objects at edge locations, so it does not reduce origin load, and it does nothing for the dynamic HTML.
choiceExplanations.3: Disabling caching increases origin load, and a bigger instance does not provide the global edge caching that reduces load and latency.

question:
A company runs three kinds of services: gRPC services over HTTP/2, standard HTTP REST services that need path-based routing, and one service that uses a custom protocol over raw TCP.
The company wants to put these services behind load balancers with the right protocol support.
Which design is MOST appropriate?
choices: Use CloudFront as the only load balancer for TCP services
Use only an ALB for all services including raw TCP
Use an ALB for HTTP/HTTPS (including gRPC) services and an NLB for the TCP service
Use only an NLB for all services and terminate TLS on instances
explanation: An Application Load Balancer is a Layer 7 load balancer that routes HTTP, HTTPS and gRPC requests by path, host or method, while a Network Load Balancer is a Layer 4 load balancer for raw TCP. Using each where it fits meets all three protocol needs.

choiceExplanations.0: CloudFront is a content delivery network for web traffic such as HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket and gRPC; it is not a load balancer and does not proxy a raw TCP service.
choiceExplanations.1: An Application Load Balancer works at Layer 7 for HTTP, HTTPS and gRPC; it cannot load balance a custom protocol over raw TCP, which needs a Layer 4 load balancer.
choiceExplanations.3: A Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4, so it could pass the traffic through, but it cannot route HTTP or gRPC requests by path, host or method, and terminating TLS on every instance adds operational work.

resources.title: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

question:
A video rendering farm runs on hundreds of EC2 instances. Each job reads large shared media files and writes per-job output files. The shared input data needs high throughput and must be accessible concurrently by all instances.
Which storage approach provides the BEST performance and simplest scaling for the shared input data?
choices: Attach one EBS volume to a single instance and share it with the fleet over NFS
Enable EBS Multi-Attach on an io2 volume and attach it to every instance
Mount an Amazon EFS file system on every instance
Copy the media to the instance store of one instance and share it with the fleet
explanation: Amazon EFS is a shared, elastic NFS file system that many instances can mount and read from at the same time, with throughput that scales and no server to manage. EBS options cannot serve a fleet of this size.

choiceExplanations.0: All traffic would pass through one EC2 instance, which becomes a performance bottleneck and a single point of failure that cannot serve hundreds of instances.
choiceExplanations.1: Multi-Attach connects one io1/io2 volume to at most 16 Nitro instances in a single Availability Zone, and it needs a cluster-aware file system, so it cannot serve hundreds of instances.
choiceExplanations.3: Instance store is temporary storage that is lost when the instance stops or terminates, and sharing it from one instance creates the same bottleneck and single point of failure.

resources.title: What is Amazon Elastic File System?
Attach an EBS volume to multiple EC2 instances using Multi-Attach

question:
A SaaS application uses Aurora and has a heavy write workload plus a growing number of read-only analytics queries. The team wants to scale reads independently and reduce load on the writer without redesigning the schema.
Which solution best meets this requirement?
choices: Add Aurora reader instances and route read-only queries to the reader endpoint, keeping writes on the writer endpoint
Enable Multi-AZ and route analytics queries to the standby instance
Increase the Aurora storage size to improve read throughput
Put an Amazon SQS queue in front of the writer instance to buffer the analytics queries
